title: Jonah Whale Rig
subject: Evidence
stem:
At a privately run Bible-story art fair held in a rented civic-center hall, Mary sued Paul for injuries she suffered when a suspended foam whale from a Jonah display dropped from its rigging. Mary testified on direct examination that Paul had climbed a ladder, loosened a support rope, and ignored Lydia’s warning to clear the aisle. On cross-examination, Paul’s lawyer asked Mary whether, shortly before the whale fell, she had eaten illegal psilocybin candies. Mary invoked the privilege against self-incrimination.

How should the court treat Mary’s claim of privilege?
call: How should the court treat Mary's claim of privilege?

choices.A: Uphold it, because Mary's credibility cannot be attacked by conduct for which she has not been convicted.
choices.B: Uphold it, because the privilege may be claimed in civil as well as criminal proceedings.
choices.C: Deny it, because Mary waived the privilege by choosing to testify in the case.
choices.D: Deny it, because whether Mary had taken the psilocybin candies is essential to judging the accuracy of her observations.

rightExplanation:
B is correct. Mary is a witness in a civil case, but the question asks whether she had engaged in illegal conduct shortly before the event she described. A truthful answer could expose her to criminal liability or supply a link toward it.

Gold Key: A witness may invoke the self-incrimination privilege in a civil case when the answer could expose the witness to criminal liability; ordinary impeachment value does not override that privilege.

Silver Key: In an outcome-plus-reason Evidence array, do not keep a choice just because it reaches the right result. The reason must match the controlling layer. Here, the controlling layer is privilege.

c3.label: CLASH
c3.text: The meaningful clash is privilege layer vs impeachment relevance. D says the question is too important to credibility to block. B says the privilege applies even in civil cases. The fact that resolves the axis is that the cross question asks Mary to admit illegal conduct.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: Apply the Gold Key. Criminal-exposure privilege beats ordinary impeachment value. Residual answer: B.

studentScript: The question is about privilege, not how useful the cross-exam would be. Mary has not opened the psilocybin subject, and the answer could expose criminal conduct, so the court should uphold the privilege. Pick B.

A.signal: It says uphold, but the reason lives in conviction-status impeachment rather than the privilege layer.
A.lawyer: Conviction status is not the controlling reason; the privilege turns on criminal exposure from the answer.

B.signal: This is the only answer that matches the privilege layer and the civil-witness posture once the Gold Key is known.
B.lawyer: The Fifth Amendment privilege may be invoked by a civil witness when a truthful answer could incriminate her.

C.signal: The choice uses the fact that Mary testified, but it skips the subject she testified about.
C.lawyer: A witness does not waive the privilege merely by testifying about non-incriminating matters.

D.signal: The choice answers the credibility/impeachment question, not the privilege question.
D.lawyer: The question may be relevant to perception, but a valid self-incrimination claim prevails over that impeachment need.

goldKeys.statement: A witness may invoke the self-incrimination privilege in a civil case when a truthful answer could expose the witness to criminal liability or supply a link in that chain. Ordinary impeachment value does not override that privilege.
goldKeys.trigger: a civil witness is asked a question whose answer would admit illegal conduct
goldKeys.unlocks: the civil-versus-criminal trap and the impeachment-necessity trap
goldKeys.authority: Fifth Amendment; McCarthy v. Arndstein, 266 U.S. 34 (1924); Hoffman v. United States, 341 U.S. 479 (1951)

goldKeys.statement: A witness does not waive the self-incrimination privilege merely by testifying about non-incriminating matters. Waiver risk appears when the witness has voluntarily opened the same incriminating subject.
goldKeys.trigger: direct testimony covers ordinary merits facts, but cross-examination moves into potentially criminal conduct

silverKeys.statement: In an outcome-plus-reason Evidence array, do not keep a choice just because it reaches the right result. Cut any choice whose reason answers a lower layer than the live privilege claim.
silverKeys.trigger: two choices uphold and two deny, each with different reasons
silverKeys.unlocks: the right-result/wrong-reason uphold choice and the dominant impeachment-relevance trap

remediation.title: Privilege Layer Before Impeachment Need
remediation.signal: Cross-exam asks a civil witness about illegal conduct.
remediation.tinyRule: Criminal-exposure privilege can block a credibility question.
